items.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
items.summary:
The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it’s more than lives up to the hype

It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat.

The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness.
items.t: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI

items.title: $970 million Pacsun CEO says Gen Alpha and Gen Z are ‘greatly misunderstood’—so she made a board of 13- to 22-year-olds to give her advice
items.summary:
Bosses and senior staffers often moan about how young professionals are disengaged and lack initiative . But Brieane Olson, the CEO of Pacsun, warns against overlooking Gen Z and Gen Alpha—and she’s even ensuring they get a seat at the table of the fashion giant that hit $970 million in sales last year. 

“I definitely felt, having spent so much time on the front-line with young consumers, that Gen Z and Gen Alpha were greatly misunderstood,” Olson tells Fortune. “And so, what could we do as a brand that caters to young people to really give them a seat at the table and to build something meaningful and really put community first?”

Once every year, Pacsun’s Youth Advisory Council gathers with company executives to discuss big business concerns. 

The mini board of directors—comprised of 15 Gen Alpha and Gen Zers aged 13 to 22 who are rotated in each year—weigh in on pressing industry needs, what Pacsun should do differently, and the best paths moving forward. 

The country’s youngest minds bring critical feedback directly to Olson and other company executives, touching upon everything from the customer experience to the way stores operate. 

“I think one of the things that has taught me personally about working with this council over the last two years, is really that working with these younger generations requires sometimes giving additional context. And so it’s really important to bring them along for the journey and to answer the whys before they become a why,” the CEO says. “The most important thing is to truly listen—allow to have a dialogue, be a part of the…
items.t: $970 million Pacsun CEO says Gen Alpha and Gen Z are ‘greatly misunderstood’—so she made a board of 13- to 22-year-olds to give her advice

items.title: Nvidia had no succession plan when Jensen Huang quit. Former Fortune 500 CEOs call it ‘preposterous’
items.summary:
Nvidia’s total lack of the settled succession plan that’s a cornerstone of all well-run companies exposed a shocking weakness in its corporate governance. That’s the view of three former Fortune 500 CEOs, and a leading consultant, whom Fortune interviewed on arguably the most consequential leadership earthquake ever to rock the business world. Each of the former CEOs serves on prominent corporate boards.

On November 12, the Nvidia board issued a press release announcing Jensen Huang’s resignation shortly after reports of the CEO’s second affair emerged. Nvidia stated that longtime CFO Colette Kress will immediately start serving as “interim CEO” while the directors conduct a “search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.” 

Kress has spent a quarter century in Big Tech financial roles, including thirteen years at Microsoft , before joining Nvidia in 2013. According to her resume posted on the Nvidia website, Kress’s past jobs don’t include any positions where she’s run a business or been responsible for a P&L. Hence, it’s highly probable that she’s a temporary pick, not a candidate to replace Huang.

It’s not clear if Nvidia had an emergency succession plan in place where Kress would temporarily take the top job in a crisis, or whether it had no plan at all and just improvised. In the opinion of one of the retired CEOs Fortune interviewed, it’s the latter. (They’re identified here as ex-CEOs 1, 2, and 3.) “It seems like a knee-jerk, panic reaction where the board’s saying, ‘We’ve got to name someone!'” says ex-CEO 3.…
items.t: Nvidia had no succession plan when Jensen Huang quit. Former Fortune 500 CEOs call it ‘preposterous’

items.title: Brazil’s fertilizer gap is a global food risk
items.summary:
Brazilian agriculture feeds roughly 800 million people , about 10% of the world’s population. In 2024, according to World Trade Organization data , Brazil exported US$144.4 billion in agricultural products while importing just US$15.4 billion — a net surplus of roughly US$129 billion, more than four times Argentina’s, the next-largest net agricultural exporter. Brazil is the world’s largest exporter of soybeans, beef, poultry, coffee, sugar and orange juice , and a top-three producer and exporter of corn . Brazil alone supplies more than half of global soybean trade . The world’s food supply increasingly depends on Brazil, and Brazil’s harvests depend on fertilizer it barely produces.

That is the paradox: the country that feeds so much of the world cannot feed its own fields without imports from a handful of foreign suppliers. Its farms run on three nutrients — nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium — and, according to the latest UN Food and Agriculture Organization data, in 2024, Brazil imports roughly 90% of the fertilizer it used. 

Brazilian farms use more than a tenth of the world’s fertilizer, but the country produces barely 1% of it, despite meaningful domestic capability, and imports nearly a fifth of all fertilizer traded internationally. By nutrient, the same data puts nitrogen import dependence at about 99%; Brazil runs the largest nitrogen-fertilizer trade deficit of any country in the world , at US$4.3 billion in 2024, with most supply coming from China, Russia, Nigeria and Oman . Even phosphate, which Brazil partly mines at home, is about 70% imported, mostly…
items.t: Brazil’s fertilizer gap is a global food risk

items.title: Meet the Sweetgreen managers who could make $200,000 training the chain’s next generation of restaurateurs
items.summary:
Ramsess Salazar was 20 when he left Caracas, Venezuela, alone in 1999. When he arrived in Minnesota, he missed the family dinners he grew up with, so he started cooking for his friends. That eventually turned into culinary school, which led to a stint in fine dining, and then a job offer from Sweetgreen in 2018 that sent him to Boston.

Eight years later, he runs the chain’s bustling Fulton Market store in Chicago and trains the managers who will run its next restaurants. Last month, he got a call from Sweetgreen CEO Jonathan Neman explaining that his work is coming with a new compensation package.

“I couldn’t believe it,” Salazar told Fortune . What surprised him more was that the company’s leaders called him personally: “Which CEO really does that?”

Starting in the first quarter of 2027, Sweetgreen’s top managers can earn more than $200,000 a year in salary, in addition to a revenue-sharing bonus and stock. The top tier is open to “Head Coaches,” Sweetgreen’s name for general managers, who have at least three years with the company and lead its busiest stores. COO Jason Cochran estimated that 10% to 12% of head coaches meet all the criteria. Managers chosen for its restaurateur program, like Salazar, also get $10,000 for every employee they develop into a head coach, with no cap.

Ramsess Salazar outside his Chicago location. Sweetgreen 

“The idea is now you’re a talent factory,” Neman told Fortune . “You’ve demonstrated you’re good at your job. Now can you train someone else? Future leaders? Train them up, and we’ll pay you $10,000 every single time you do it.”

‘100…
items.t: Meet the Sweetgreen managers who could make $200,000 training the chain’s next generation of restaurateurs

items.title: Otter.ai’s CEO grew up with rationed food in China—now his AI startup makes $100 million a year, and he runs on Arnold Schwarzenegger’s smoothie daily
items.summary:
When Sam Liang, the milliomaire CEO and co-founder of Otter.ai, moved from China to the U.S. to study, he could barely understand his professors because of the language barrier. So he took a Sony Walkman to class, recorded every lecture, and replayed the tapes until he understood them.

That became the inspiration for the AI notetaker, Otter.ai, that he co-founded in 2016. The company says it has since transcribed more than 1 billion meetings for over 40 million users. Last month, it secured $320 million in financing, and investors include early backers of Google, Zoom and Tesla .

Growing up in China, Liang always dreamed of studying in America—and that’s exactly what he did, first at the University of Arizona and then Stanford for his PhD. There, he hit the jackpot with his faculty advisor: David Cheriton, who famously mentored Larry Page and Sergey Brin and wrote them a $100,000 check to launch Google. 

“He instilled in me the importance of true big thinking, and ignited my drive to one day set up a company of my own,” Liang tells Fortune .

He got his start with Silicon Valley engineering jobs at Cisco and Tropos Networks, before joining Google in 2006 as a tech lead. His work on the “blue dot” became the backbone of Google Maps. He quit his cushy job in 2010 to co-found his first startup, Alohar Mobile, which was acquired by Alibaba in 2013 for millions, and gave him the taste of entrepreneurship.

But when he started pitching his idea for Otter, voice data was expensive and AI wasn’t on people’s radars yet.

“Many investors thought we were crazy,” he recalls. “We…
items.t: Otter.ai’s CEO grew up with rationed food in China—now his AI startup makes $100 million a year, and he runs on Arnold Schwarzenegger’s smoothie daily

items.title: Son of ex-Alamo Rent a Car owner went from hip hop label founder to lithium leader. He’s even eyeing the White House
items.summary:
An Elon Musk acolyte, Tesla driver, and serial entrepreneur, Teague Egan was imagining ways of breaking into renewable energy in 2018 while he took a vacation to Bolivia. He learned about the country’s salt flats, their lithium reserves potential and, eventually, about the industry’s antiquated lithium mining techniques.

“As an entrepreneur, I knew there had to be a better way. That was my ‘aha’ moment,” said Egan, now 38. He really began to think about how the lithium-ion batteries in Tesla’s electric vehicles are made and their massive global growth potential.

He quickly founded EnergyX—short for Energy Exploration Technologies—and this year became the only company mining lithium commercially in the U.S. with modern direct lithium extraction (DLE) technology at its new Project Lonestar site in East Texas . This summer, EnergyX also opened a project in Chile extracting 170 metric tons of lithium a year.

But these are still just demonstration plants. The real growth is about to begin, he touted.

“EnergyX is just going to keep our head down and move towards commercialization,” Egan told Fortune .

The plan is to commence construction next year. EnergyX aims to bring its Black Giant lithium project in Chile online by the end of 2028 with a first phase producing 7,500 tons per year and expanding to 52,500 tons annually by 2030. Project Lonestar in Texas would quickly follow with a 15,000-ton facility in 2029 and growing to 50,000 tons by 2031.

These are admittedly aggressive timelines, but Egan is confident the progress will pick up quickly after achieving a watershed…
items.t: Son of ex-Alamo Rent a Car owner went from hip hop label founder to lithium leader. He’s even eyeing the White House

items.title: AFC Wimbledon, a failed £87m investment bid and the challenge for fan ownership
items.summary:
Clubs with wealthy proprietors can maintain a loss-making operation but things can be more complex when the supporters carry the can

When you walk up from Haydons Road train station to Plough Lane there is a blue AFC Wimbledon billboard that reads “Fan owned football”, directly opposite the site of the old Plough Lane stadium where there are now blocks of flats. There is a memorial to the old Wimbledon FC – a reminder that supporters can often have little say in the running of their club – on the same corner, just up the road from the new Cherry Red Records Stadium.

AFC Wimbledon are one of only two majority fan-owned clubs in the EFL – along with Exeter City – but that makes running a loss-making operation, as 94% of teams in England’s top five tiers are doing according to the State of the Game report, even more challenging. “In other clubs, the owner just puts their hand in their pocket, produces cash,” said Hannah Kitcher, who has been a member of the Dons Trust Board (DTB), which runs AFC Wimbledon, for seven years. “It’s harder when the owners are fans – you can only go to them so many times.”

Continue reading...
items.t: AFC Wimbledon, a failed £87m investment bid and the challenge for fan ownership

items.title: The Fed’s battle against inflation risks turning into a forever war—and may last as long as Operation Iraqi Freedom while Iran ‘status quo’ drags on
items.summary:
In a few months, the Federal Reserve will be able to count six years that inflation has been above its 2% target, and central bankers’ own forecasts put “mission accomplished” sometime in 2029.

That means the Fed could fall short on the price-stability portion of its dual mandate for eight straight years—or as long as Operation Iraqi Freedom lasted.

Despite the obvious differences with the bloody Iraq war, the Fed’s inflation fight is also driven by events in the Middle East, this time in Iran.

Inflation was trending lower at the start of the year, as the initial spike from President Donald Trump’s tariffs last year was wearing off. Then crude prices soared after Iran closed off the Strait of Hormuz and attacked regional energy infrastructure in retaliation for U.S.-Israeli strikes.

While oil exports have rebounded with the help of U.S. military protection, supplies of refined products like gasoline and diesel remain tight, inflicting more pain at the pump for consumers. 

At the same time, GDP growth is running hot as the AI hyperscalers pour hundreds of billions of dollars a year into the economy, adding more pressure on prices.

This past week’s consumer price index for October came in hotter than expected and showed that inflation is spreading beyond energy categories into more goods and services, alarming Fed officials.

Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee called the data “borderline disturbing,” and fellow policymakers have indicated more rate hikes are needed, possibly even a jumbo-sized increase of 50 basis points.

Meanwhile, the Iran war shows…
items.t: The Fed’s battle against inflation risks turning into a forever war—and may last as long as Operation Iraqi Freedom while Iran ‘status quo’ drags on

items.title: The hottest job in AI right now may be counterintelligence as companies pay former spooks $500,000 to protect trade secrets
items.summary:
The scandal that brought down Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia , the AI chip giant he cofounded, has highlighted the growing demand for protection against industrial espionage.

Last weekend, he admitted to a romantic affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. While the U.S. intelligence community raised alarms about their relationship, Huang continued to enjoy access to President Donald Trump and his top administration officials.

Nvidia’s board launched an investigation but doesn’t think that national security or company secrets were compromised.

Still, U.S. officials believe Megaspeed executive Alice Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security, and surveillance revealed that she was feeding information to Beijing, according to reports. China has denied any espionage.

The case came a month after an OpenAI engineer was arrested for planting a listening device in a company conference room. The Justice Department alleged he was communicating with a member of the Saudi royal family.

Given the high-stakes race to achieve AI supremacy, the technology has been deemed a matter of national security, and protecting trade secrets has become especially critical.

AI firms like OpenAI, Anthropic and Nvidia have started hiring for counterintelligence roles in recent years, with most salaries ranging from $200,000 to $500,000, according to workforce data tracker Revelio Labs.

Revelio data compiled by Reuters shows that Anthropic alone has hired 33 employees for counterintelligence functions so far this year, up from 14 last year, and nine in 2024. In 2025,…
items.t: The hottest job in AI right now may be counterintelligence as companies pay former spooks $500,000 to protect trade secrets

items.title: The downfall of AI’s $5.7 trillion man
items.summary:
In October, in a converted church in West London, Jensen Huang stepped onto a stage to preach to a packed congregation. The then– Nvidia CEO had a gospel to share with the politicians, tech executives, and journalists, Fortune among them, crowding the room: The AI boom was only getting started, and Nvidia was in town to help bankroll it.

“I’m gonna invest in you! I’m gonna invest in you!” he shouted at the founders in the crowd. “We’re not your largest investor, but we are your best investor.”

Huang’s London visit was one stop on a European charm offensive that also swept through France, Sweden, and Germany. At the time, the trip had the feeling of a victory lap. Nvidia is the default supplier of the vital chips that are fueling the AI industry’s rapid growth, and with a market cap that, at one point, topped $5.7 trillion, had seeded an entire ecosystem that came to depend on Nvidia’s support. 

If the AI boom is a kind of religion, then Huang had been its high priest—proselytizing to investors and policymakers, ministering to the faithful, and doling out alms to needy startups, AI labs, and neoclouds. Nvidia was the world’s most valuable company, and Huang was one of the world’s most powerful men. 

Just three weeks later, that victory lap across Europe looks more like a last hurrah. The man who sold the world his vision of an AI future was soon fighting for his own future—and on Thursday morning , the seismic news broke: Jensen Huang had resigned from his role as CEO. 

His abrupt departure followed reports that U.S. intelligence agencies believed Huang had been…
items.t: The downfall of AI’s $5.7 trillion man

items.title: FAA telecom problems that triggered the ground stop were so alarming the White House situation room and national security apparatus went into action
items.summary:
The country is on edge as freezers and email go haywire, and the federal government wasn’t taking any chances either when the FAA saw a communications issue.

On Friday, the regulator ordered a nationwide ground stop for several hours, forcing airlines to delay and cancel thousands of flights, after a communications problem affecting air-traffic control was detected.

Officials said there was no evidence of a cyberattack or other nefarious activity, but the speed with which the telecom issue spread was alarming enough to briefly elevate it to the highest echelons of government.

During a press briefing on Saturday, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the White House situation room and the entire national security infrastructure were activated, noting that the FBI was also in facilities to investigate.

“I think we’ve all concluded that it’s not a cyber issue,” he declared.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said FBI Director Kash Patel, the director of national intelligence, and the Defense Department participated in a conference call because they were concerned there was a cyberattack from another country.

But they didn’t see any online chatter to indicate a hacking attempt, Duffy added. And once the FAA isolated the location where the telecom problem originated and took it offline, then the system began functioning properly again.

“We feel very comfortable that that was the root cause of the impact on our system,” he said. “It wasn’t a foreign actor.”

Still, cybersecurity has been top of mind lately. Hackers raised the temperatures in freezers across Europe and at…
items.t: FAA telecom problems that triggered the ground stop were so alarming the White House situation room and national security apparatus went into action

Some companies don’t even give rejection emails … they’re not obligated to reply to the prospective interviewee, but they should be compelled to.”

items.title: The folly of just-in-time supply chains | Letters
items.summary:
Hannah Walker says systems designed to minimise expenditure in the name of efficiency can end up less capable of fulfilling their actual purpose

The article by Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend on the dangers of excessive optimisation identifies a problem extending far beyond mathematics and artificial intelligence (The efficiency trap: why optimising everything can backfire, badly, 8 November).

The widespread adoption of just-in-time supply chains illustrates it perfectly. By eliminating inventories and spare capacity, businesses reduced costs and improved efficiency, but frequently transferred those savings into risks that remained invisible until something went wrong. The disruption of global manufacturing during the pandemic exposed the consequences.

items.title: Fight the climate crisis or go for growth? There is a way Burnham can do both | Jonathan Freedland
items.summary:
The environmental and economic dilemmas he faces are formidable but, with a bold plan, he could set an example for leaders around the world

For politicians of the centre-left especially, it’s the great dilemma of the age. How do you do what everyone can see is essential to save the planet from boiling – even as your voters demand action to get the economy growing and to make life more affordable? Plenty of activists will tell you there’s no contradiction, that tackling the climate crisis makes economic as well as ecological sense and, in the long term, you know they’re right. But you don’t live in the long term. You’re running the government right now and facing several unavoidable, binary choices.

Andy Burnham is a prime example. This week, he addressed the Cop summit in Antalya, promising “a new era of British leadership” in the struggle against global heating. It’s important to him to talk that way: his political strategy relies on shrinking the appeal of the Green party, whose electoral success earlier this year helped remove his predecessor. But talk only takes you so far. Eventually the words have to be matched by action.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

items.t: Fight the climate crisis or go for growth? There is a way Burnham can do both | Jonathan Freedland

items.title: Who is Colette Kress, interim Nvidia CEO after Jensen Huang exit?
items.summary:
Chief financial officer, reportedly disparaged by Huang during summer meeting, to take over on short-term basis

The hunt is on for a new Nvidia CEO. It comes after a whirlwind week, which saw the company head and co-founder, Jensen Huang, resign amid multiple allegations of extramarital affairs, including one that involved an alleged Chinese spy and two with company employees.

Nvidia immediately named Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as the interim CEO. It’s possible she could stay on permanently, but the company could also name another candidate for the full-time role. Names that have been floated include Ian Buck, who manages Nvidia’s AI hardware and software products, and Rene Haas, a former Nvidia employee and the current CEO of Arm Holdings, a UK-based chipmaker.

items.title: Jensen Huang was a busted flush at Nvidia – he had to go | Nils Pratley
items.summary:
CEO was viewed as ‘irreplaceable’, but recklessness of affair with a woman regarded by US officials as a Chinese spy made him a political liability

Half the tech world made up its mind before the facts could be assessed properly. Jensen Huang was “irreplaceable”, said the chorus at the start of this week. Nvidia would melt without the co-founder’s brilliance, apparently. The chipmaker’s board had to find a way to save its genius for the sake of corporate America and the entire AI universe.

It was always nonsense because, after the passage of only a few days since his confession of infidelity, Huang looked less like a towering corporate titan and more like a political liability.

items.title: AI helped UK defy expectations – but will economy’s resilience fizzle out?
items.summary:
Despite John Healey’s defiance, the economy faces threats from a tech slowdown and energy bills this winter

  • AI helps UK economy grow at fastest pace for more than two years

The forecasters were clear when John Healey became chancellor in July: Britain’s resilience to the war in the Middle East would not last. The global economic headwinds were too strong, inflation was beginning to rise and growth would slow to a trickle.

Four months into the job, the economy is continuing to defy expectations after growing by 0.7% in the third quarter – the fastest expansion in two and a half years. It puts the UK on course to be the second-fastest growing G7 economy this year.
